questions.title: Layered carbon in an electrolytic cell
questions.stem: A graphite electrode is made from the material shown. The short in-layer C–C distance is 142 pm and the separation between layers is 335 pm. The electrode is then used in molten PbBr₂ with inert electrodes.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the two distances numerically and explain what the difference indicates about the interactions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how graphite can conduct parallel to its layers and why the layers can slide.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write both electrode equations for molten PbBr₂ and identify the electrode where oxidation occurs.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Determine the mass of lead when 0.0250 mol Br₂ is collected under conditions of complete product recovery. Use M(Pb)=207.2 g mol⁻¹.

steps.text: 335/142≈2.36; the interlayer spacing is about 2.36 times the bond length.
Within a layer, strong covalent C–C bonds form a network.
Between layers the attractions are weaker London forces; the dotted lines do not represent further covalent C–C bonds.
Each carbon bonds to three neighbours, leaving electrons delocalized across its layer.
Delocalized electrons carry current, while weak interlayer attractions allow layers to slip.
Cathode: Pb²⁺+2e⁻→Pb.
Anode: 2Br⁻→Br₂+2e⁻.
Oxidation is loss of electrons by bromide at the anode.
The electrode reactions require equal amounts of Pb and Br₂, hence 0.0250 mol Pb.

questions.diagramCaption: Stacked sheets of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons within each graphite layer.

questions.title: Analysing a gas blend
questions.stem: A 100.0 cm³ mixture contains only CH₄ and C₂H₆. Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives 145.0 cm³ of dry CO₂. All gas volumes are compared at the same temperature and pressure; water is removed before measuring CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write balanced equations for complete combustion of each hydrocarbon.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the volume percentage of each hydrocarbon.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the oxygen volume consumed and the volume remaining if the original oxygen supply was 300.0 cm³.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A leak removes some CO₂ before its measurement. Explain the error in the inferred ethane percentage and one way to check the collection apparatus.

steps.text: CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O.
2C₂H₆+7O₂→4CO₂+6H₂O.
Let x be ethane volume, so methane volume is 100.0−x.
CO₂ volume=(100.0−x)+2x=145.0, hence x=45.0 cm³.
45.0% ethane and 55.0% methane by volume.
Methane uses 2×55.0=110.0 cm³ O₂.
Ethane uses 3.5×45.0=157.5 cm³ O₂; total=267.5 cm³.
Remaining oxygen=32.5 cm³.
A lower CO₂ yield is interpreted as less of the two-carbon gas; ethane fraction is underestimated.
Pressure-test the sealed apparatus or pass a known gas volume through and measure its recovery.

questions.answerSummary: Pressure-test the sealed apparatus or pass a known gas volume through and measure its recovery.

questions.title: Ammonia and a strong acid
questions.stem: A flask contains 40.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). It receives 30.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Assume acid transfer to NH₃ is quantitative, volumes are additive, and remaining strong acid controls final pH.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the proton-transfer equation using H₃O⁺ and identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the limiting reactant and the amount of excess strong acid.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the final pH. Explain why simply averaging the initial pH values would fail.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain the origin of the new N–H bonding pair when NH₃ accepts a proton.

steps.text: NH₃+H₃O⁺→NH₄⁺+H₂O.
NH₄⁺/NH₃ is one conjugate pair.
H₃O⁺/H₂O is the other.
The 1:1 transfer makes NH₃ limiting.
Excess strong acid=0.00150 mol.
Acid–base reaction changes amounts; pH is logarithmic and cannot be averaged by volume.
Both electrons originate from the nitrogen lone pair, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

questions.answerSummary: Both electrons originate from the nitrogen lone pair, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

questions.title: Reversing a dissolution measurement
questions.stem: A 5.00 g salt sample, molar mass 80.0 g mol⁻¹, dissolves in 95.0 g of water in a cup. The temperature falls from 23.40 to 20.10 °C. Approximate solution c as 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect cup heat capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the heat change of the solution and the molar enthalpy of dissolution.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the sign using the competing energy changes when an ionic solid dissolves.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Each temperature reading has maximum uncertainty ±0.05 °C. With other quantities exact, estimate the maximum percentage and absolute uncertainties in ΔH.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: If heat enters from the warmer surroundings during dissolution, explain how the reported ΔH changes.

steps.text: Separating ions from their lattice requires energy.
Hydration of ions releases energy, but the net endothermic result shows the energy requirement exceeds the energy released.
Maximum uncertainty in the fall is ±0.10 °C.
Relative uncertainty=0.10/3.30×100=3.03%.
Absolute enthalpy uncertainty≈0.67 kJ mol⁻¹; accept ±0.7.
Heat entering offsets some of the temperature fall.
The inferred positive dissolution enthalpy is smaller than its true magnitude.

questions.answerSummary: The inferred positive dissolution enthalpy is smaller than its true magnitude.

questions.title: Following a four-carbon alcohol
questions.stem: A compound with formula C₄H₁₀O contains one hydroxy group. On controlled oxidation it gives a ketone. Compare straight-chain alcohols only.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the alcohol and the ketone by name and condensed structural formula.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the oxidation equation using [O] and show the change in oxidation state of the carbon bearing OH.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give the names and condensed formulas of the two successive oxidation products of its straight-chain primary alcohol isomer.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why butan-2-ol has a higher normal boiling temperature than an ether of similar molar mass that lacks an O–H bond.

steps.text: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
Butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃.
The OH-bearing carbon is bonded to two carbon groups, so this secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃+[O]→CH₃COCH₂CH₃+H₂O.
In the alcohol that carbon has one C–O and one C–H bond; contributions +1 and −1 give 0.
In the ketone the C=O contributes +2, a rise from 0 to +2.
Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, from butan-1-ol.
Butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, on further oxidation.
Butan-2-ol molecules can donate and accept intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
A pure ether lacks an O–H donor; its intermolecular attractions are generally weaker here, requiring less energy for vaporization.

questions.answerSummary: A pure ether lacks an O–H donor; its intermolecular attractions are generally weaker here, requiring less energy for vaporization.
